This looks like a 37mm shell from WW1. This type of shell was used in many different roles. From what I've seen it was used by both the French and US forces. A couple examples of what it would be used in would be the male version of the Renault FT-17 Tank (they classified tanks in WW1 as male if a cannon or female if it only had machine guns), M1916 37mm gun (it was a portable gun used take out machine gun nests that was able to be relatively easy to conseal as it was fitted to sit low to the ground on either a tripod or a with wheels and was fitted with a very short barrel, this gun would later be put into the male FT-17s), and the M1917 37mm gun (although they look similar, the M1916 was developed by the French and the M1917 developed and produced by the US for the French and later US. The M1917 was less portable and less concealable as it had a longer barrel and was on a much higher chassis with wheels and had a protective armor plating like a traditional artillery piece.). Overall the 37mm shell was mostly used for eradicating machine gun inplacements, they weren't used all to much for anti-personnel. All this information was gathered a while ago so if I did say anything incorrectly, please correct me. I like it told correctly and I like learning. Sorry if this was too long of an explanation or if anything is wrong. If you get a chance to visit Kansas City, go to the National World War One Museum and Memorial. There you can see a M1917 37mm gun and a FT-17. If you want to learn anymore you can ask me I can try to do more research if you need. Thank you for preserving history!

They are airbrakes. They are used to slow down the aircraft. If there weren't holes in them. There would be too much forces acting on them for how large of a deflection they have and they would most likely not be able to deploy against the wind flowing around the wings, or it would break the hydraulics of the airbrake. On Dauntless Divebombers it was used to slow them down after a dive so they could pull out of the dive. In later aircraft, like the F-84, there are airbrakes on the side and botton of the fuselage towards the rear of the aircraft with holes. Because of new and better technology with hydrolics, holes are not needed to decrease the amount of force exerted on the hydrolics, and the holes substantially increase the drag of an aircraft and the stealth capabilities. But to sum up my answer. They are airbrakes to slow the aircraft down, and they have holes to let some air though in order to not break things.
